That inference is wrong. The variable was never the platform, it was test ORDER: the replay table is a module-global `OrderedDict` with a 900 s TTL and the suite had no global isolation for it, while `test_session_intents.py:43` and `test_loop_control_contention.py:125` share the literal key `a1b2c3d4-0000-4000-8000-000000000001`. When xdist lands both files on one worker, the second file's `halt_save` POST REPLAYS the first file's stored answer and performs no side effect, so `os.replace` is never called and cycle 26's injector correctly reports `0 matching attempts`. **It reproduces on Windows in 1.8 seconds** - `pytest tests/test_session_intents.py tests/test_loop_control_contention.py -q` gives 1 failed / 54 passed - which is the measurement that kills the OS framing. Cycle 26's guard was right, cycle 26's mechanism was right, and the explanation attached to the residual was wrong; the guard fired for a reason nobody had looked for. RM-281's own first hypothesis was the closer one ("no write ever happened, and the context-exit assertion masked the reason") and it was half right - the POST did not fail on Linux, it succeeded as a replay returning HTTP 200 with `replayed: true`.

**FIXED STRUCTURALLY, NOT PER FILE - BECAUSE THE PER-FILE FIX ALREADY EXISTED AND IS WHY THE CLASS STAYED OPEN.** The correct isolation had been sitting at `tests/test_loop_control_idempotency.py:56` since S2, an autouse fixture whose docstring already says "The replay table is process-global - isolate every test". A guard one file opts into does not cover the file nobody has written yet, so this went into `tests/conftest.py` as an autouse fixture alongside the ones that already reset process-global state there. A cross-file sweep then measured the real size of the class: **3 keys colliding across 4 test files**, the other two (`test_interrupt_route.py` against `test_loop_control_idempotency.py`) previously safe only because both of those files happened to carry their own fixture. `skipif` was never on the table - RM-281 explicitly prohibits it and `feedback_unrun_gate_is_where_the_bug_hides` is the reason - and the guard still runs on Linux.

**THE AUDIT FINDING IS BIGGER THAN THE CI RED, AND IT DEFEATS THE MODULE'S ENTIRE PURPOSE.** `_apply_idempotent` was `idem.seen(key)` -> side effect -> `idem.remember(key, payload)`. `seen` and `remember` are each locked; the SEQUENCE is not. `dashboard/server.py:54` is a `ThreadingHTTPServer`, so two requests carrying the same key run on two threads, both read an empty table, and both act. The module's own docstring says why that matters: "`interrupt` itself is the most important entry in the list, because a phone retrying over Tailscale must not kill twice." **A retry storm from a wedged client is CONCURRENT, not sequential** - so the shape the gate defended was the one that does not happen, and the shape that does happen was undefended. Proven with a red-first test before any fix: two threads, one key, a side effect held open on an Event, and the assertion `both threads ran the side effect - the gate is not atomic` fires on the unfixed code.

**THE FIX IS AN ATOMIC CLAIM, AND IT PRESERVES THE OLD WIRE CONTRACT EXACTLY.** `claim(key)` decides replay / act / wait under one lock and returns `("hit", result)`, `("claimed", None)` or `("inflight", event)`; the winner owns the key and finishes with `settle` (HTTP 200) or `abandon` (anything else, plus an `except BaseException` unwind so a raising side effect can never strand a claim). A waiter blocks on the owner's Event - bounded by `INFLIGHT_WAIT_S`, 2 s - then re-claims, inheriting the owner's settled answer with `replayed: true`. The "only settled 200s are remembered" rule is unchanged, so an abandoned 400/503 still lets the next caller act. No lock is ever held across a wait, and `clear()` now WAKES its waiters rather than orphaning them, which would otherwise turn a cleared table into a mysterious stall instead of a failure.

**THE IN-FLIGHT TIMEOUT DELIBERATELY RETURNS 200 + `ok:false`, NOT 503, AND THAT IS A FINDING NOT A PREFERENCE.** `web/mc/mc.js:51-53` maps EVERY HTTP 503 to the literal "auth not configured on the server" and returns before `r.json()`, discarding the server's payload. A 503 here would have told the operator their auth was broken when the request was merely still running. Filed as **RM-283**, because the same mis-mapping already misreports a real lane-launch failure the same way - a friendly message that is actively wrong, which is the CLAUDE.md Error Handling rule inverted rather than obeyed.

**ONE HOLE IN MY OWN DESIGN, STATED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER.** If `MAX_ENTRIES` (512) distinct keys are remembered between an owner settling and a waiter waking, the settled answer is evicted and the waiter - which cannot distinguish an evicted key from an abandoned one, since both must mean "act" - runs the side effect twice. It needs 512 distinct intents inside one wake-up on a single-operator local surface, and the pre-claim code had the identical hole through `seen()`, so it is a bound to know about and not a regression. The alternative is an outcome flag carried on the Event, which is machinery for an unreachable case. The comment at `MAX_ENTRIES` says all of that.

(B) replacing `abandon` with `settle` on the non-200 path -> the abandon test goes RED because the waiter never got to act. **THE ROW WAS RIGHT ABOUT THE HEADLINE AND WRONG ABOUT ITS SECOND HALF, AND THE WAY IT WAS WRONG IS THE MORE USEFUL FINDING.** RM-255 stated `certifi` "appears in NEITHER `requirements.txt` NOR `requirements.lock`, so the `_SSL_CONTEXT` built from it is `None` in the shipped environment". The verifying grep returned nothing because **`requirements.lock` is UTF-16LE**: BOM `ff fe`, does not decode as UTF-8 at all, and `grep -c certifi requirements.lock` returns **0** against a file that plainly contains the string. `feedback_empty_grep_is_a_claim_about_the_pattern`, landing on a dependency audit. The true defect is narrower and still real: certifi is UNDECLARED in `requirements.txt`, the file CI actually installs, so on CI the context IS None - the CA-store hardening worked on one box by accident, through another package's dependency chain. Declared it directly (already in the lock, so no lock regeneration). The UTF-16 lock became **RM-273**.

**THE HEADLINE, MEASURED BEFORE ANY EDIT.** With the blocklist file missing, `is_blocked("https://reddit.com/x")` returned **False**; with a half-written file, **False**; and starting from a good file, one truncating write flipped a live client from True to **False** - because `_maybe_reload_blocklist` re-runs on EVERY call, so a single mid-write `stat` latched the fail-open. A control that silently allows everything is not a degraded control, it is no control. Now: **fail CLOSED** when nothing was ever loaded (every url refused until the file is repaired), and **last-known-good RETAINED** when a previously good list goes bad - never silently widened, and deliberately not fail-closed there, because converting a transient mid-write into a total outage of all outbound fetching is the wrong trade. Shape is validated too: `{"hostnames": "reddit.com"}` used to be iterated CHARACTER BY CHARACTER into a set of single letters that blocks nothing, and `{"hostnames": [123]}` raised `AttributeError` straight out of the constructor.

**THREE BYPASSES, EACH ONE CHARACTER OR ONE HOP WIDE.** (1) A trailing dot: `reddit.com.` is a legal FQDN that resolves identically, and it defeated BOTH halves - it is not in the host set and `"site.ru."` does not end with `".ru"`. (2) Scheme: the default opener carries `FileHandler`, so `file://localhost/C:/Windows/win.ini` was a LOCAL FILE READ through what every caller believes is an HTTP client - and one slice agent found it gets worse, the bytes are read into the response body and the call only THEN dies at `resp.getheaders()`, so the disclosure completes before the crash, and `AttributeError` is neither `OSError` nor `URLError` so it escapes both handlers and the breaker never records it. (3) Redirects: the blocklist was consulted only on the initial url, and the default opener follows 302s, so an allowed host could redirect straight to a blocked one. Fixed with host normalization on BOTH sides, an `ALLOWED_SCHEMES` allowlist, and a per-client opener whose redirect handler re-checks every hop.

**THE BREAKER DID NOT DO WHAT ITS OWN DOCSTRING PROMISED, AND THE SLICE CORRECTED MY DIAGNOSIS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS.** The docstring claims "half-open after 60s; one probe call closes it on success"; there was no probe marker anywhere in the class, so every concurrent caller was admitted at once. Worse, and found by the slice rather than by me: `_on_failure` only stamped `opened_at` when it was `None`, which an open breaker never is - so **a failed probe never restarted the cooldown and the breaker became a permanent no-op against a permanently-down host**. My D1 claim was PARTIALLY REFUTED: `_check_breaker` never read `st.failures` at all, it read `opened_at` twice unlocked, and the real consequence is `now - None` raising `TypeError` out of a method whose declared failure mode is `CircuitOpen`. Now a true one-probe half-open under `st.lock`, with the rate limiter moved to its OWN lock so a thread sleeping up to a second in the rate gate no longer stalls breaker bookkeeping for that host.

**TWO DEFECTS IN MY OWN FIX, BOTH CAUGHT BY THE AGENTS I ASKED TO CHECK IT.** (a) I cached the failed file's mtime to avoid a log flood - which means a writer that truncates and then finishes inside the SAME filesystem tick leaves a perfect file the client never re-reads: a PERMANENT fail-closed outage, strictly worse than the fail-open being fixed. My own probe missed it because it forced a distinct mtime with `os.utime` - a fixture shaped to the bug. Fixed by not trusting the mtime while degraded, plus log-once-per-transition. (b) I added a probe slot without guaranteeing its release: `http.client.IncompleteRead` is an `HTTPException`, so it escapes every handler and would leave `probe_in_flight` True, wedging that hostname `CircuitOpen` for the life of the process. Fixed with a `settled` flag and a `finally`, checked rather than cleared unconditionally so it can never release a slot another thread was admitted into.

**MUTATION: 12 MUTANTS, 12 KILLED, ZERO SURVIVORS, EVERY RESTORE SHA256-VERIFIED, AND THE FIRST PASS FOUND REAL GAPS.** The first 9 killed only 7. Both survivors were genuine holes in the agent-authored tests: the empty-string filter in `_parse_blocklist` (a single stray `""` in `suffixes` makes `endswith("")` true for every host - one typo denies the entire internet) and the scheme guard in `request()`, which is very nearly an EQUIVALENT mutant since `is_blocked()` also refuses the scheme and only the MESSAGE differs. DONE **2026-08-30 (lane 8 Headless-True-Audit cycle 26: this lane's own regression corpus used the OPERATING SYSTEM as its fault injector, so the retry path in the repo's atomic-write primitive had never once executed on Linux; Tier-1).** Target: the nine CI-red tests across five lane-8-authored test modules, plus the shared fault-injection contract underneath them. **Closes RM-270**, filed by lane 8's own cycle 25 one cycle earlier. **Selected on criterion 5 (repeat offender)**: the failures had accumulated across cycles 12, 13, 20, 21 and 23, and the branch could not merge.

**THE PICK WAS MADE BY PRE-FLIGHT, NOT BY THE MENU.** `gh run list` at pre-flight showed `lane/true-audit` red. Reading the failed log rather than inheriting a verdict showed all nine failures were tests LANE 8 ITSELF had written. The lane's own wrap step requires green CI before declaring done, so five consecutive cycles had each declared done over an inherited red they had each contributed to. **The mandatory `perseus_recall` did NOT surface RM-270** - it was filed the same day and the vault is a mirror that had not been re-synced, so the row was found by reading `BACKLOG.md` during the write-up. Recall is necessary and was not sufficient here; the durable lesson is that a same-day row is invisible to recall by construction.

**ONE ROOT CAUSE, NOT NINE BUGS.** Four of the nine reproduced a failed atomic write by opening the destination file and letting the OS supply the fault: `with open(target): assertRaises(PermissionError)`. On win32 an open read handle share-locks the destination so `os.replace` raises WinError 5; on POSIX the rename goes straight through. All three affected modules were traced to ONE choke point rather than assumed to share one - `performance_tracker.py:13`, `core/decision_detector.py:47` and `dashboard/routes_loop_control.py:94` all import from `core/polled_json`, reaching `_write_then_replace` -> `_replace_with_retry` -> `os.replace`.

**THE FINDING THAT IS WORSE THAN THE RED, AND IS WHY A SKIP PASS WOULD HAVE BEEN THE WRONG FIX.** A test ASSERTING the failure goes red on Linux and is visible. A test asserting only the CLEANUP AFTER a failure goes **vacuously green** there, because no fault ever occurred and there was nothing to clean up. Those never appear in a failure list at all, which is why the count kept growing unnoticed. **Measured: 8 of the 12 converted tests were in the vacuous class, not the red one** - two thirds of the damage was invisible. The consequence is that the exhaustion branch of `_replace_with_retry`, the re-raise in the primitive every polled writer in the tree funnels through, had never executed on a Linux runner. Its failure path was covered only by an accident of Windows file-locking.

**RM-270 OFFERED (a) SKIP / (b) A WINDOWS CI JOB / (c) ASSERT THE INVARIANT, AND RECOMMENDED (c). THIS RUN INDEPENDENTLY CONVERGED ON (c) AND THEN SPLIT THE NINE.** For the four replace-semantics failures plus the eight vacuous siblings, option (c) verbatim: `tests/_replace_faults.replace_fails` injects the fault at the `os.replace` boundary, so the retry loop, the backoff, the scratch-file cleanup and the re-raise run identically on every platform, and the assertions that were always the point (no orphaned tmp, a 503 not a 500, one decision logged once, the prior file intact) are unchanged. **Coverage went UP, not down:** the exhaustion path is now executed on Linux for the first time. The narrow question that really was OS-shaped - does a held handle still share-lock a destination here - became three separate platform-gated tests asserting only that, so the simulation cannot quietly diverge from the real OS. For the surrogate-token failure, (c) as well: the property (an unencodable configured token yields a clean 401, never a 500) is platform-independent, and only the DELIVERY was Windows-only.

**THE FIVE OCR FAILURES ARE THE HONEST EXCEPTION, AND ARE RECORDED AS SKIPS RATHER THAN DRESSED AS (c).** `pytesseract` is absent on the runner, so `handle_ocr` returns `{"error": "pytesseract/PIL missing"}` at `vision_server/_inference.py:351-352` before any crop is touched. That is a capability gap, not a platform semantic, and no invariant rewrite can make an OCR test meaningful without an OCR engine. They are skipped on a predicate that performs **the same imports the production guard performs, in the same order**, with a skip reason that names the gap so a CI log cannot read as a silenced failure. **The skip is deliberately per-test, not per-class**, because `handle_ocr` validates body SHAPE before importing the OCR stack by design (its own comment at `:331-334`), so the pre-import guards must keep running on a stack-less box - and they do: 32 passed under simulated absence.

**THREE FINDINGS THE SLICE PRODUCED THAT NOBODY WENT LOOKING FOR.** **(1)** A sixth OCR test, `test_undecodable_crop_is_skipped_not_raised`, was GREEN on CI and vacuous: without the stack, `.get("result", {})` is `{}`, so `assertNotIn("gold", ...)` passed while proving nothing. Gated and strengthened with an error-count assertion so removing the gate fails loudly. **(2)** The merger's own stated acceptance - "the pre-import tests still passing proves you did not over-skip" - **was false as written**, and the agent said so rather than satisfying it: those tests asserted only `assertIn("error", r)`, which the ImportError short-circuit also satisfies, so they would have passed with their guards deleted. Three assertions were tightened to pin the exact error token, which is what makes the un-skipped coverage real. **(3)** `test_reasonable_crop_is_still_processed` was vacuous on Legion too - a refused crop and a crop that OCRs to nothing both return `{"ok": True, "result": {}}`. Rewritten to spy on `pytesseract.image_to_string` and assert the crop actually reached OCR at `(360, 120)`.

**A PRODUCTION CHANGE WAS PROPOSED BY THE MERGER AND REFUSED BY THE AGENT, CORRECTLY.** The merger observed that the `ImportError` path returns without `_record(ok=False)` while every other early-return failure path records, and asked for an adjudication. The agent declined on three grounds and filed it instead (**RM-272**): the premise was inaccurate (`:343-344`, the `no crops` path, also returns unrecorded, so the ImportError path matches its real neighbour); recording there would make the `assertGreater(_errors(...))` tests green on a stack-less box for the WRONG reason, fenced only by a skip decorator a later edit could remove; and a missing stack is a static machine fact, not a per-call event, so recording it per call would flood an 80-entry log ring with a permanent condition and displace genuine transient errors. **Zero production files were modified this cycle** - verified by `git hash-object` against `HEAD` for all six touched during mutation testing.

**MUTATION TESTING CAUGHT TWO THINGS THAT PASS COUNTS COULD NOT.** Agent C's first mutation **did not apply** (CRLF line endings, `s.count(old) == 0`) and the suite reported a clean 18 passed - the `feedback_mutation_that_fails_to_apply_looks_green` trap exactly. The anchor assertion caught it; the pass count never would have. Agent B found an **equivalent mutant** (`_OCR_MAX_CROPS` 12 -> 999 survives because the fixture is sized `_OCR_MAX_CROPS + 5` and scales with the mutant) and swapped the mutant rather than the test, per `reference_mutation_survivor_may_be_equivalent`. A third survivor was analysed and correctly ruled equivalent: the scratch-cleanup line is unreachable from the transient-contention test by construction.

**THE ROOT-CAUSE HALF: A RATCHET, PLUS A HELPER THAT CANNOT PASS VACUOUSLY.** `replace_fails` **raises on exit if it never fired**, so a wrong path, a writer that stopped routing through the primitive, or a future refactor fails loudly instead of producing the silent green that caused this whole class. `tests/test_atomic_write_fault_injection_is_portable.py` is an AST ratchet against the idiom; its docstring states exactly what it does NOT catch (indirect writes through a route handler, handles opened via a thread or fixture, non-test modules) so the name cannot overclaim, and its `test_writer_list_covers_the_polled_json_surface` fails if `core/polled_json.py` grows a public writer the guard does not name, so the ratchet cannot quietly stop ratcheting. **Its own self-test found a real bug in it** (a `relative_to` crash on the tmp fixtures), which is the argument for writing one.

**THE MERGER RE-DERIVED ONE ASSERTION THE AGENT FLAGGED, AND THEN TESTED THE RE-DERIVATION.** Three exhaustion tests hardcoded `attempts == 4`, coupling them to the backoff table having exactly 3 entries; a deliberate table change would have turned them red and invited someone to "fix" the number. Rederived as `len(_REPLACE_RETRY_DELAYS_S) + 1`. That introduces a tautology risk - an empty table makes the expectation 1, which a single attempt satisfies - so it was **tested rather than reasoned about**: mutating the table to `()` still produced 9 red, because the transient tests catch it. The risk is real, bounded and covered.

**THE REPO'S OWN SKIP-HYGIENE GUARD REJECTED THE FIRST GATING AND WAS RIGHT.** The three real-OS tests originally gated on an imported `WINDOWS_SHARE_LOCKS` constant. `tests/test_skip_condition_hygiene.py` failed them all three as `UNRESOLVED: nothing resolvable`: it resolves a skip only when the condition names `sys.platform` / `os.name` / `platform.system` DOTTED at the site (`_PLATFORM_DOTTED`, `:846`), and treats anything else as an always-passing guard. The named constant was more readable and less checkable. Fixed by inlining the dotted form; the constant was then dead and was removed rather than left as an unused export, along with its now-stale docstring reference. **Excusing the guard was considered and rejected** - self-excusing a hygiene guard is the exact anti-pattern this cycle exists to close (`reference_guard_can_be_green_while_self_excusing`).

**ACCEPTANCE, MEASURED BY THE MERGER RATHER THAN INHERITED FROM THREE AGENTS.** One combined probe applied the CI divergences at once (pytesseract unimportable with PIL present, `os.replace` instrumented to count real share-locks) and ran all five files plus the guards: **112 passed, 6 skipped, 4 deselected, 0 failed**, against 9 failed before, with **`real os.replace share-lock PermissionErrors = 0`**. 112 + 6 + 4 = 122, matching the Windows run exactly. On a real Linux runner that projects to **112 passed / 10 skipped**: the 6 capability gaps plus the 4 win32-gated real-OS tests, which skip there by construction and are deselected here rather than faked (forcing `sys.platform` on Windows breaks pytest's own `tmp_path_factory`, which takes the POSIX branch and calls the absent `os.getuid`). An agent's report of a `tests/conftest.py:199` Windows-only defect was **REFUTED** on the same evidence: `os.getuid` exists on real Linux, and the Linux CI run executed that autouse fixture across 30061 passing tests.

**THE VERIFIER CAUGHT THREE OVERCLAIMS IN THIS SLICE'S OWN EVIDENCE, AND ALL THREE WERE THE MERGER'S.** (1) The probe's docstring claimed to hold `os.environ` to the POSIX encoding rule; it did not - the class was defined and never used, and `pytest_configure` only self-tested an unused helper. (2) There were **FOUR** win32-gated tests, not three: `test_windows_environ_really_can_hold_an_unencodable_token` RAN under the probe, so the first reported figure of 113/6/3 was wrong and a third number (`113 passed, 9 skipped`) had already reached `BACKLOG.md`. Re-measured to 112/6/4 and corrected in all three documents - the `feedback_parallel_slice_counts_jointly_wrong` shape, caught before the commit rather than after. (3) "0 real share-lock PermissionErrors" proves less than its name: the counter instruments `os.replace` ONLY, so a test depending on Windows refusing `os.unlink` or `os.rename` on an open handle would report zero and still be Linux-red. None currently does, but the claim is now scoped to what was measured.

Capped at 200, oldest-first, because a `start_matchmaking` queued twenty minutes ago must not fire when the agent reconnects. **(W6)** the self-read throttle measured a pure INTERVAL on the WALL clock, so a backward NTP step makes the difference negative, which is always under the threshold, disabling the self-heal for the length of the step. Moved to `time.monotonic()`; `ts` itself deliberately stayed wall-clock because it crosses a process boundary and every consumer compares it against their own `time.time()` (that residual is RM-269).

Secret handling is N/A on a positive basis: the module contains zero references to key material. Lock discipline is clean and was checked rather than assumed - no lock is held while another is acquired (`threading.Lock` is not reentrant, so a nested acquire would hang), and `_maybe_self_read` releases its throttle lock before the network read. Stating the trust boundary precisely is what keeps the severity of everything above honest: the realistic adversary here is a sibling agent on its own release cadence, not an anonymous remote caller.

Two writers of one file therefore opened the SAME scratch file: B truncates and renames it while A is still filling it, and A's remaining bytes land in the published destination. **Measured on win32 before any edit, two threads writing one file, 240 writes: 5 reads returned unparseable JSON, plus 3 FileNotFoundError and 3 PermissionError on the writers themselves.** A torn destination is precisely the failure this module's docstring promises cannot happen ("readers see either the old content or the new, never a partial write"). **Reachability is not hypothetical and it is worse than RM-254 recorded:** `data/force_scan.json` has FOUR independent writers - `core/hotkeys.py:103`, `dashboard/_writers.py:68`, `coaches/arena_coach.py:481` and `tools/lcu_agent.py:1372`, the last in its own process (`RC-LCUAgent` ONLOGON task) - with a live reader at `coaches/_base_coach.py:465`; and `coaching_data.json`, the most-polled file in RC, has two (`app/__init__.py:253` and `dashboard/_writers.py:44`). Fixed with `_scratch_path` returning `<name>.<pid>.<token>.tmp` as a SIBLING of the destination (rename is only atomic within one filesystem). **The pid is load-bearing, not decoration: the colliding writers are separate processes, which is exactly the case no in-process lock can serialize.**

**W4 shipped WITH W5 because fixing W5 alone makes W4 worse.** An exhausted retry re-raised and orphaned the scratch file. That was survivable while the name was fixed - the next write reused it - but a per-writer name turns the same leak into unbounded litter. `_write_then_replace` now removes it on every failure path, under `except BaseException` so a KeyboardInterrupt mid-write cleans up too.

**W1 (the contract module violating its own docstring, with three consumers already documenting the bug).** `read_json_dict` promises the default when a file is "missing, unreadable, or stores something other than a dict". It caught `(FileNotFoundError, OSError)` and `json.JSONDecodeError` - but `read_text` raises `UnicodeDecodeError`, which is a `ValueError`, NOT an `OSError`, so a non-UTF-8 polled file raised straight through the promise. **The striking part is that this was already KNOWN downstream and never fixed upstream:** `core/cost_tracker.py:491` spells it out ("swallows OSError + JSONDecodeError but lets UnicodeDecodeError (ValueError) escape on a non-UTF-8 ledger") and `coaches/_base_coach.py:502` and `:540` each widened a handler to absorb it. Three consumers documented the resolver's defect in prose and compensated locally - `feedback_resolver_fix_is_not_a_consumer_fix`, in the direction where the evidence was sitting in the codebase the whole time. All three comments were corrected in this slice, because they now describe behaviour that no longer exists.

**W2 / W3 (the shared-mutable defect class, in the contract module).** `read_json_dict` returned `dict(default)` - a SHALLOW copy - so a caller appending to a returned `{"log": []}` poisoned the caller's own default object AND every later call that passed it. `PolledJsonFile.__init__` had the same shallow copy. Both now deep-copy. This is the same defect cycle 22 fixed in `coaches/sr_user_builds`, found one layer down.

**THE MUTATION PASS FOUND TWO PROBLEMS AND ONE OF THEM WAS MINE.** 12 mutants, restore sha256-verified after each. First run: 10 killed, 2 survived. **M8** (reverting the `PolledJsonFile.__init__` deep copy) survived because `read()` delegates to `read_json_dict`, which now deep-copies anyway - so the constructor's copy was unguarded, not equivalent: it still controls whether construction takes a SNAPSHOT or a live view of the caller's dict. That earned a real test rather than a shrug. **M10 was a badly-built mutant of my own** - I "mutated" a line by appending a comment, which changes nothing; rebuilt as three real mutants returning the caller's `default` by reference from each of the three fallback branches, which in turn exposed that my W2 test only covered the missing-file branch. Parametrizing it across missing / malformed / non-dict / undecodable is the fix, and is exactly `feedback_guard_on_nondefault_call_path_is_untested`. Final: **12/12 killed.**

**I DID NOT MEET RM-254's ACCEPTANCE ON THE FIRST PASS AND READING THE ROW IS WHAT CAUGHT IT.** RM-254 asks for "a two-process (not two-thread) test that the destination is never torn". I had written a two-THREAD test. Two tests were added: `test_a_separate_process_picks_a_different_scratch_name`, which compares the scratch name a child process chooses against this process's for the same destination and is **deterministic** (RED under a revert to the shared name), and `test_two_processes_writing_one_file_never_tear_it`, the behavioural contention check. **The second is recorded as a SMOKE test, not a guard, because it was measured: against the same revert it went RED on only 1 of 2 attempts.** It stays because it asserts an absence the fix makes structurally impossible, so it cannot flake red in CI; it is simply not something to rely on. The same honesty applies to its two-thread sibling, which passed pre-fix. **Reading the acceptance criteria of the row you are closing is the cheap step that turns a plausible closure into a real one.**

**THREE CONSUMERS MIRRORED THE OLD SCRATCH NAME AND TWO OF THEM BECAME SILENT NO-OPS.** `dashboard/routes_loop_control.py:177-186` unlinked `<dest>.tmp` after a failed write with a comment reading "Must mirror atomic_write_bytes' own tmp naming"; `performance_tracker.py:60-67` did the same - **written by lane 8's own cycle 23, five commits earlier on this branch**. Both would have kept looking like cleanup while unlinking a name that no longer exists, and `missing_ok=True` means it breaks quietly. `dashboard/_writers.py` hand-rolled the whole pattern (it deliberately keeps `ensure_ascii=True`, which is why it does not call `atomic_write_json`); its serialization stays local and only the tmp+rename is delegated. `coaches/arena_coach.py:481` was converted too - it was the third `force_scan.json` writer, hand-rolled, with no retry at all. **A helper's callers can encode assumptions about its PRIVATE naming; changing the private detail silently breaks them.**

**BACKFILL (6e): measured EMPTY, and the probe is the evidence.** The already-bad state for these defects would be stray scratch files and torn or non-UTF-8 polled files in the live tree. Scanned the live `C:\Riot Commander`: zero `*.json.tmp` / `*.txt.tmp` under the data and runtime roots, and every polled file under `data/`, `ops/runtime/` and `coaching_data.json` decodes as UTF-8 and parses. **FILED, NOT FIXED: RM-261 / RM-262 / RM-263 / RM-264.** RM-261 is the sibling grep this lane mandates: **96 modules hand-roll the same destination-derived scratch name**, and fixing the contract module reaches NONE of them. (4) My W2 narrative read as an observed incident when it was a probe - no production caller passes a nested-mutable default - so both W2 and W3 are recorded as LATENT exposure, corrected in the docstring rather than left to imply an outage. **THE SEVEN DIMENSIONS, each with a verdict (section 8).** **4a CORRECTNESS - HARDENED:** the docstring made two claims that were both false and both provable by test ("never a partial write", "always returns a dict"); a third, the `PolledJsonFile` lock scope, was corrected as prose. **4b SECURITY - HARDENED (narrow):** the only trust boundary here is disk content, and `read_json_dict` is it - decode, parse and type are now all validated at that boundary instead of one of them escaping. **W1 (HIGH, silent loss of the user's rating).** `_atomic_write_json:34` ended in a BARE `os.replace`, while `core/polled_json.py:30-35` already records that `os.replace` transiently raises `PermissionError` (WinError 5) on Windows whenever a concurrent reader holds the destination open, that these files are polled by design so the contention is routine, and that the identical retry ALREADY SHIPPED to `ops/rc_supervisor.atomic_write_json` on 2026-05-02. This module simply held a PRIVATE COPY that never received it - `feedback_resolver_fix_is_not_a_consumer_fix` in its plainest form. The reader is real and cross-process, not hypothetical: `agents/supervisor.py:794-805` imports `performance_tracker._latest_rating_file` and `read_text()`s the winner, and `ops/phase3_install.ps1:57` launches that supervisor as its own process. **Measured on Python 3.14 / win32, same conditions, two writers:** against a reader that released after 80 ms the bare writer raised in 0.6 ms while `core.polled_json.atomic_write_bytes` rode it out and landed its content; under a permanently held handle BOTH raise, the hardened one after ~278 ms. That separation is the whole experiment and the honest limit is recorded with it - the retry buys the TRANSIENT window only, exactly as that helper claims, and no more. **The failure was triple-masked, which is why it sat here:** the raise is caught at `:361` and only WARNED; control falls THROUGH so the MatchDB row at `:386` is still written and `app/_game_lifecycle.py:236` then logs `"Performance rating saved"`; and the stale file keeps its stale MTIME, so `_latest_rating_file` still selects it and the post-game summary silently enriches from a PRIOR game. **W2 (HIGH, silent loss of the grade AND the match row).** Every numeric read used `game_state.get(key, default)`, which supplies the default only for a MISSING key and passes a present-but-NULL value straight into the arithmetic. **Measured: all six of `ally_kills_total`, `cs_per_min`, `gold`, `game_seconds`, `deaths`, `kills` crashed `save_rating` with a `TypeError`** - `game_seconds` on the very first line, via `is_valid_match`. The upstream Live Client feed is one RC does not author and has changed shape before. Fixed with a `_num` coercion at the boundary, applied in `is_valid_match`, the `stats` dict, the `gpm` divisor and the `kp` divisor. **`app/_game_lifecycle.py` is FROZEN, so the coercion had to live here - which is the correct place for it regardless, and no frozen file was touched this cycle.** **The sibling sweep the fix would have missed:** grepping the module for other feed-supplied numeric reads AFTER the `save_rating` fix found the same root cause live in `save_tft_rating` - a null `alive_others` crashes the placement derivation, and a null `stage` crashes the `0<stage<=4` compare in `calculate_tft_rating`. That matters more than the original, because TFT is 8041 of the 8395 rows in the live store. **The `stage` case also carries a probe trap worth keeping:** it is reachable ONLY when `stage_round` fails to parse, since a parsed `stage_round` leaves `sn` truthy and the fallback never runs - so the natural probe, with a well-formed `stage_round`, reports OK and hides the crash. A test with an injected raiser proves the handler WOULD leak - it wrote `key=sk-ant-FAKE-TESTKEY-lane8-cycle23` into an `rc.tracker` log record. **But the live path is REFUTED as reachable, for two independent measured reasons:** `experimental_builder._call_haiku` catches everything at `:236` so no anthropic exception escapes `record_result`, and the SDK's own `str` / `repr` / `%s` / traceback surfaces were probed against a stub 401 and a connection refusal (anthropic 0.96.0 / httpx 0.28.1) and carry no credential - only a deliberate walk of `exc.request.headers` exposes it. The redaction shipped anyway as DEFENCE IN DEPTH because the margin is one formatting change wide: `repr()` of the `UnicodeEncodeError` raised by a non-ASCII key file DOES embed the key, so changing that line to `%r` or `logger.exception` would have leaked it. Recorded this way deliberately - `feedback_verified_claim_vs_measured_downstream`: the function-level leak is real, the live-reachability inference from it would have been wrong.

**The finding, measured not reasoned.** `_awrite` (`:147-151`) hand-rolled `tmp.write_text(...)` + a BARE `os.replace`, while its OWN docstring said "loop_controller polls mid-write" - naming the exact condition under which Windows raises `PermissionError` (WinError 5), because a reader holding the destination takes a share lock. `core/polled_json.py:39` `_replace_with_retry` has existed for this the whole time and its comment calls the contention "routine"; `dashboard/_writers.py:29-36` already records a MEASURED instance caused by a plain `open(target, "r")`. The contention is not hypothetical here: `STOP` is read from three poll loops - `loop_controller.py:772/786` every 5 s, `claude_gui_bridge.ahk:299` every 1 s, and `routes_loop_status.py:450` `read_text()` on every browser poll (`web/mc/mc.js:885`, 5 s). Proven with a throwaway probe BEFORE any edit: `stop` under a held reader raised `PermissionError [WinError 5]`, the catch-all at `:480` turned it into HTTP 500 `"internal error - see logs"`, the halt did not land, and `STOP.tmp` was stranded - which `test_loop_control_route.py::test_atomic_no_tmp_left` exists to forbid but never catches, because it never drives the contended path. A guard on a call path no test exercises, again.

**Five defects fixed, all in-slice.** (1) `_awrite` routes through the NEW `core.polled_json.atomic_write_bytes`, which reuses `_replace_with_retry`; `atomic_write_json` / `atomic_write_text` are UNCHANGED, so no existing caller's bytes moved. (2) The same call writes BYTES, not text: `Path.write_text` was rewriting LF as CRLF, so the route reported `17 chars queued` while putting 19 bytes on disk, and `MAX_DIRECTIVE` was not a byte cap (`reference_windows_write_text_crlf_byte_count`). (3) When the ~275 ms backoff legitimately exhausts, the route now cleans its own tmp and returns a **503 with an actionable line** - `"control file busy - the loop is mid-poll, retry"` - instead of a generic 500; the operator has to be able to tell "your halt did not land, press it again" from "the server is broken" (CLAUDE.md Error Handling: friendly message out, raw cause to `logs/`). (4) `_steer` caught only `ValueError` / `OSError`, but `ops/loop/steer.py:146` serializes on a Win32 named mutex and raises `winmutex.MutexTimeout`, a **RuntimeError** - so losing a 5 s lock race became a 500; it is now a scrubbed 503. (5) `interrupt_preview`, documented "Read-only" and "Kills nothing, writes nothing", ran `CONTROL_DIR.mkdir` before its own early-return and created the directory; the mkdir moved below it.

**Seven dimensions: 5 HARDENED, 1 CLEAN, 1 N/A.** CORRECTNESS/SECURITY/ERROR-HANDLING/RESOURCE-LIFETIME/INPUT-VALIDATION HARDENED; CONCURRENCY **CLEAN** (`_inference` writes no polled file, and its only shared-state mutator `_stats._record` is `_stats_lock`-guarded at `vision_server/_stats.py:39`, as is `_get_client` at `_config.py:65` - so the atomic-write rule has nothing to bite on here); PATH-TRAVERSAL **N/A** (the module builds no filesystem path from request data; the only literal is `_TESSERACT_DEFAULT`).

**Six defects fixed in-slice, each measured before it was written up.** **(1) A non-dict model answer was counted GREEN.** `_parse_json` is annotated `-> dict | None` and has been since it shipped, but `json.loads` on `[1,2,3]` / `123` / `"x"` / `true` returned that value straight through; `handle_vision` then took the `result is not None` branch and recorded `_record("vision", ok=True)`. **Blast radius CONTAINED and stated as such:** both live consumers already isinstance-gate the value (`modes/shared_vision.py:383` `return result if isinstance(result, dict) else None`, `dashboard/_screen_read.py:134`), so nothing crashed - the harm is that a failed read was counted a success in `/stats` and cached 2 s by `core/moon_proxy.py`'s dedupe. The first draft of this finding claimed a downstream break; opening the consumer refuted it. **(2) `resp.content[0].text` assumed a non-empty content list whose FIRST block is a text block** - measured: empty content raises `IndexError`, a leading thinking block raises `AttributeError`, the exact class CLAUDE.md's Error Handling rule names. Replaced with `_first_text()`, which scans for the first block carrying a `str` `.text`. **(3) A merely-WRONG body raised out of all three handlers** - `[1,2]` on `/vision`, `/coach` and `/ocr`, `crops="stage_round"` (where `in` succeeds on a str and indexing does not), a non-str `image_b64`. Each became a bare HTTP 500 via `_err500`, and because the raise preceded `t0`, **not one reached the stats ring** - malformed traffic was both mislabelled and invisible. Now a named error plus `ok=False`. **(4) `_crop_to_primary`'s except-handler was itself a crash** - it called `.startswith` on the same non-string whose `b64decode` had just raised, so the RECOVERY path raised. **(5) The model id was fully caller-controlled with no validation.** A membership allowlist was considered and **REJECTED with a reason**: `modes/shared_vision.py:273` legitimately sends `SONNET_MODEL` and `tft/` sends its own, so pinning to `VISION_MODEL`/`COACH_MODEL` would have broken the escalation path this server exists to serve - the narrow-first-fix failure of item 208. `_MODEL_RE` validates SHAPE instead. **(6) OCR memory amplification, MEASURED not asserted:** `_pre` upscales every crop 3-4x LINEAR (9-16x in pixels) with no bound - a 5 KB 1000x1000 PNG became a **16 MB** resident buffer at scale=4, ~3000x wire-to-memory under a 10 MiB body cap, and a 9000x9000 crop sits just under PIL's 89 MP threshold and reaches ~1.3 GB on a `ThreadingHTTPServer` worker. Capped at `_OCR_MAX_CROP_PX = 4096` / `_OCR_MAX_CROPS = 12`, dimensions read BEFORE any allocation. `TypeError`, `MemoryError` and `DecompressionBombError` (a direct `Exception` subclass, covered by NO entry in the old tuple) were added to `_OCR_EXC`, and the unconditional `_record("ocr", ok=True)` now reports `ok=False` when every attempted crop threw.

**Two ROOT-CAUSE SIBLINGS found by grep and fixed in the same slice** (CLAUDE.md "Engine / Build Conventions"): `vision_server/_frame.py:231` guarded the JSON DECODE but not the SHAPE, so valid-JSON-but-not-an-object reached `.get` and raised - on the frame-upload path the coaches poll every 2 s; and `vision_server/_relay.py:49` returned `f"bad_json: {e}"`, **echoing the decoder's byte offset and document context to the caller** and bypassing the redaction `_err500` applies to every RAISED error - the same leak class cycles 18 and 19 closed in `routes_diag` and `routes_state`. That fix needed a second correction: `log` was not imported in `_relay.py`, so the first version would have raised `NameError`.

**Mutation-tested: 17 mutants, 16 RED individually, 1 proven equivalent.** Removing the `_pre` isinstance guard ALONE survived, and the honest reason is defence in depth - `TypeError` in `_OCR_EXC` independently catches it. Rather than delete the test or claim a pass, the COMBINED mutant (both guards removed) was run and goes RED, so the pair is jointly load-bearing and the single-guard mutant is equivalent (`reference_mutation_survivor_may_be_equivalent`). **Three tests were worthless on the first mutation run and were rewritten**: `assertNotIn("gold", result)` passes whether the oversized crop is REFUSED or merely unreadable, so it survived the removal of the very cap it was written for (`feedback_negative_assertion_rules_out_without_pinning_down`). They now assert the discriminating observable - the stats ring counts a refused crop as a FAILURE and an illegible one as a clean read - and the bomb branch is pinned end-to-end by temporarily lowering `Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`. Every restore in the harness is sha256-verified (`reference_backup_path_or_fallback_breaks_restore`).

**One self-inflicted regression, caught by the baseline and fixed.** `_OCR_EXC` referenced `Image.DecompressionBombError` at runtime, and `tests/test_p2w1_app_a.py` substitutes a `types.SimpleNamespace` for the PIL Image module, so the tuple build raised `AttributeError` - `test_handle_ocr_runtime_passes_timeout_value` went red. Resolved defensively via `getattr`; the guard is still pinned because its own mutant re-run goes RED against real PIL. **The pre-edit baseline is what made this provable rather than arguable:** taken BEFORE any edit at 2 failed / 19386 passed, and the new failure was NOT one of those two names.

**Machine environment (4g), re-measured live, and it BOUNDS every severity above.** `Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 8889 -State Listen` reports **`127.0.0.1`** on pid 12148 - loopback only, not the `0.0.0.0` that item-1177 recorded, so RM-150's bind fix is confirmed still holding and these defects are NOT LAN-reachable the way cycle 19's `:8888` findings were. No `RC-VisionServer` scheduled task exists, consistent with its 2026-06-11 removal; `dashboard/server.py` is the sole launcher.

Its 139 ERROR lines are ALL upstream Anthropic errors - `529 overloaded_error`, `500 api_error`, `400 Could not process image` - correctly routed to the log by `_err500` rather than to the caller, which is the existing architecture working. So there is no corrupted state to repair, and the `400 Could not process image` line is separately logged as corroboration for RM-247.

DONE **2026-08-30 (lane 8 Headless-True-Audit cycle 19: `dashboard/routes_state.py` served raw exception text at eight sites on a LAN-reachable port, died with NO HTTP RESPONSE on a truthy wrong-typed field, let one malformed queue line report a failing agent6 as GREEN, and let an unauthenticated POST write ANSI escapes into the operator's terminal log; Tier-1).** Target `dashboard/routes_state.py` (1189 lines at start, `frozen=no`), chosen on criterion 1 (it hosts the `/api/input` and `/api/command` POST handlers the lane mandate names explicitly), criterion 4 (1189 lines against two narrow test modules, neither a contract suite) and criterion 5 (the highest repeat-offender count of any candidate - 24 `docs/LEDGER.md` + 39 `docs/history_notes.md` mentions). **EIGHT defects fixed in-slice, all measured, all TDD, all mutation-tested.** **(1) The raw-exception-into-the-body class, at SIX sites in `/api/health/all`** - five `{"error": str(e)[:120]}` sub-probes (vision, Daemon Slayer, supervisor, cost, agent6) plus `"last_error": task.get("last_error")` with NO cap at all. This was LIVE, not theoretical: the running dashboard served **227 characters of raw `claude` CLI stderr** naming an auth env var under `agent6.last_outcomes[].last_error`. **The RM-134 guard NAMES this module and cannot see it** - `test_every_dashboard_importer_gets_the_scrubbed_helper` asserts only `mod.send_error is send_error`, i.e. that the module IMPORTS the scrubbed helper, never that it USES it (`reference_guard_domain_narrower_than_its_name`, and the same shape as cycle 18). All six now render `GENERIC_ERROR` and log the raw cause; the serving boundary also re-scrubs, because a future edit to the producer must not be able to reopen it. Fixing only the two sites I first spotted would have been the classic too-narrow fix - the other three were found by the sibling sweep the rewrite loop mandates. **(2) TWO MORE raw-error sites in the same file** (`_serve_ui_version`, `_serve_ds_preview_post`), both `str(exc)[:200]` into the body while their siblings used `send_error` correctly for the SAME input - `_serve_ui_version` additionally had NO log call at all, so its failure was wholly unobservable. **I missed both in my own sibling sweep because I truncated the grep with `head -25`** and this file sorts after `routes_peel_priority`; a parallel agent caught them. A truncated grep is a claim about your pager, not the codebase. **(3) A truthy wrong-typed field killed the handler with NO HTTP RESPONSE AT ALL.** `.strip()` sat outside the try in both POST handlers, so `{"text": 123}` or `{"command": {"a":1}}` raised an uncaught `AttributeError`, the worker thread died and the socket closed with zero bytes - the browser sees a network error, not a 400. Only FALSY wrong types were safe (`[]`, `0`, `null`, `{}` fall through `or ""`), which is why it survived. **It survived LEDGER 1181 because that fix is a CONTAINER check and `{"text": 123}` IS a dict**; its test parametrizes only whole-body shapes, never a field type. **(4) A length cap on `/api/input`** - nothing on the path bounded it (`_writers.set_pregame` and `core.coaching_payload.pregame` both uncapped), so one ~1 MiB POST inflated EVERY `/api/state` response and SSE frame at 2 Hz across up to 8 subscribers, and survived restart because it lands on disk. Disk-fill is REFUTED (the field is overwritten, not appended). **(5) One malformed line flipped the health dot from yellow to GREEN.** The scan validated JSON SYNTAX but never JSON SHAPE, so a line parsing to a non-object made `ev.get` raise, and the `except` sits OUTSIDE the per-line loop - one bad line aborted the scan for the whole 4.6 MB file. Because the caller keeps the TAIL, the entries lost were always the most RECENT ones, exactly the failures the yellow dot exists to report. **(6) A FAILED scan also read as green** - a distinct defect my first fix did not cover, and one an independent agent caught: `[]` from an unreadable file was indistinguishable from `[]` meaning "clean history". `_agent6_audit_outcomes_ex` now returns `(outcomes, scanned_clean)` and the rollup reports the honest third state `unknown`; the list-only wrapper keeps the historical contract so existing callers and tests are unchanged. **(7) ANSI control-character injection into `logs/`.** `/api/console-error` wrote six request-controlled strings into the daily log with no escaping, so an unauthenticated POST could embed a screen-clear escape to wipe the operator's terminal and write a forged, genuine-looking WARNING line - or a bare newline to forge a whole record. `_handler._scrub_log` is the in-tree helper for exactly this; cycle 13 used it for the `log_message` override and the sweep never reached here. **(8) `dashboard/_writers.atomic_write_json` had no WinError-5 retry** - the module docstring cites the CLAUDE.md atomic-write HARD rule and the implementation used a bare `tmp.replace(p)`. MEASURED on this machine: a plain read-mode `open()` by a reader is enough to raise `PermissionError [WinError 5]`, leaving an orphan `.tmp`; the operator-visible symptom is the dashboard Refresh button returning `500 {"error":"command_failed"}` and doing nothing. Now reuses `core.polled_json._replace_with_retry` (bounded ~275 ms, then re-raise) rather than re-rolling the backoff table, and unlinks the tmp on failure. Serialization deliberately NOT delegated to `polled_json.atomic_write_json`, which passes `ensure_ascii=False` and would change the bytes for non-ASCII coaching text. **This is the one file beyond the audited module that this slice touches, and it is a callee not a caller** - taken because it is where the HARD rule is broken for the canonical polled file the audited handlers write.

**A criterion-4 claim of my own was WRONG and is corrected here rather than repeated.** My selection scan reported "zero dedicated test file" from `ls tests/ | grep`, which does not descend into subdirectories. The honest count is **7 test modules plus one fixture** touching the module (`phase2_smoke/test_snapshot_translation.py`, `snapshot_regressions/test_app_authority.py`, `snapshot_regressions/test_snapshot_authority.py`, `test_jade_coach_path.py`, `test_liveclient_championstats_ingestion.py`, `test_p2w1_app_a.py`, `test_silent_except_liveclient_subresource.py`, `fixtures/state_dicts.py`). There is still no `tests/test_snapshot_normalizer.py`, which is the true and narrower statement.

**TWO CRITICALS, both wrong on REAL unmodified Riot data in EVERY game, and neither is the numeric class I went in for.**

**(1) Every turret kill was credited to CHAOS.** `_calc_objectives` read `team = ev.get("TowerTeam", ev.get("TeamID", ""))`. **Neither key exists in the Live Client eventdata schema** - repo-wide, `TowerTeam` appeared on that one line and NOWHERE else, while the rest of the tree already parses the structure NAME (`dashboard/_liveclient.py:348-350`, and real `Turret_T2_L_03_A` names appear in `tests/test_district_fusion.py:159`). So `team` was always `""`, and the `elif CHAOS` and the `else` incremented the SAME counter - meaning `_order_towers_down` was structurally pinned at 0 for the life of the process and an ORDER player was told they had lost zero towers in a game they were losing on structures. Fixed with a new `_turret_side()` that parses the token against the authority already in the tree, `core/district_fusion.py:85` `_SIDE_BY_TOKEN = {"T1": "ORDER", "T2": "CHAOS"}` (which names whose structure DIED). An unrecognised name now credits NEITHER side - laundering the unknown into a real count is precisely what caused the defect, so `test_unparseable_turret_name_does_not_silently_credit_a_side` pins that.

**(2) A respawned jungler stayed flagged dead, so the gank-threat field announced "SAFE".** `_update_enemy_tracking` popped `_enemy_death_time` when the record said dead, but cleared the record's own `dead` flag only INSIDE `if x or z:` - which a champion who has respawned and is walking back through FOG never satisfies, because the Live Client reports position (0, 0) for an unseen player. The record therefore stayed `dead=True` indefinitely, `_gank_threat` emitted `SAFE - <jungler> is dead` about a living jungler, and `_derive_enemy_locations` discarded a perfectly good last-seen zone as `untracked`. This is the most dangerous single inversion available in that field. Fixed by clearing the flag unconditionally at the pop; `test_still_dead_enemy_is_still_reported_dead` is the control proving a genuinely dead enemy still reads dead.

**The root cause I went in for: the wire-numeric hardening was applied to exactly ONE field and never to its siblings.** `_coerce_num` exists (its docstring records that `json.loads` accepts the bare NaN/Infinity literals, and that the primary relay path `game_reader/poller.py:155` calls `_process_game` UNWRAPPED). It was applied to `currentGold` and to the 20 `championStats` fields - genuinely the best-hardened block in the file - and to nothing else. Measured against the real `_process_game`: `scores.creepScore = "50"` raised `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for /: 'str' and 'float'` at the `cs_per_min` division, and `None` did the same. `_respawn_secs` indexed `_RESPAWN_BASE[min(level, 18)]`, clamped at the TOP only, so **level -1 returned 54 - the LEVEL-18 respawn, the maximally wrong answer** - while a float level raised on list indexing and a str/None raised on the `min()`. Fixed root-cause-first with a new `_coerce_int` applied at 11 READ sites (cs/kills/deaths/assists, my_level, both `_safe_kills`-style accumulators, the `elv >= my_lv + 2` comparison, both respawn reads, the enemy/ally level detail lines), plus a both-ends clamp inside `_respawn_secs` as defence in depth. `_safe_kills` was misnamed: it guarded that `scores` is a dict, never that `kills` is numeric.

**I OVERCLAIMED THE HEADLINE AND MEASUREMENT KILLED IT - recorded because it is the part worth keeping.** I framed the NaN half as "a poisoned `creepScore` makes `json.dumps` emit a bare `NaN`, so the browser's `JSON.parse` rejects the ENTIRE `/api/state` document and every panel dies". The `json.dumps` half is true and I demonstrated it. The consequence is FALSE: `cs_per_min` never reaches `/api/state` as a raw number, and its only route into `app.data` is `StateAuthority.calc_win_pct`, where `app/_state_authority.py:79` computes `min(10, max(-10, ...))` - and `max(-10, nan)` returns `-10` (measured directly, not reasoned). NaN is clamped away before the browser sees anything. The real residual is much narrower: a NaN reaches the Haiku prompt as the literal `nan`. The test docstring was rewritten to say so before commit. The CRASH half needed no downgrade and in fact got WORSE on inspection: the raise escapes into `core/sr_aram_worker.py:204`, which logs at DEBUG only, `none_streak` sits in the `else` branch and so never increments, no game-end signal fires, and **the dashboard keeps rendering the last good state as if live, indefinitely**.

**A SURVIVING MUTATION WAS PROVEN EQUIVALENT AND THE TEST GUARDING IT WAS DELETED, NOT PATCHED.** M7 reverted the `max(0, ...)` clamp on `ago` in `_derive_enemy_locations` and all tests stayed green. Rather than invent a test, I checked the mechanism: that site's buckets are `< 8` visible, `< 45` MIA-with-seconds, else MIA, and EVERY negative value lands in the same `< 8` bucket as the clamped 0 - verified exhaustively over -10000..-1, zero differing inputs. 1282. DONE **2026-08-30 (lane 8 Headless-True-Audit cycle 16: `core/match_db.py` wrote the empty STRING into thirteen INTEGER/REAL columns, which broke `get_mode_stats("TFT")` outright and defeated the `tft_placement > 0` guard; ALL 8395 live rows were affected and are now repaired; Tier-1).** Target `core/match_db.py` (282 lines, `frozen=no`), chosen on criterion 1 (it persists Riot/LCU match data RC does not author), criterion 3 (SQLite under WAL with per-thread connections, 9 non-test consumers) and criterion 4 (**zero dedicated test file** - `ls tests/ | grep match_db` was empty). Confirmed NOT among the 15 files taken in cycles 1-15. Perseus recall returned no CLOSED/REFUTED row for it; the one relevant hit (`sqlite-wal-per-call-connections-on-windows-serialize-writes`) describes per-CALL connects, which this module does not do.

**The root cause is one line.** `save_match` built its bind dict as `{c: data.get(c, "") for c in cols}` - every absent column defaulted to `""` regardless of declared affinity. SQLite converts a numeric-LOOKING text value but stores a non-numeric one AS TEXT, so a TFT save (which carries no kills/cs/gold) wrote `''` into thirteen numeric columns. **Two consequences, both measured against the live 17 MB DB, not reasoned about.** (1) **`get_mode_stats("TFT")` raised `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'` unconditionally** - `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM matches WHERE mode='TFT' AND typeof(kills) IN ('integer','real')` returns **0 of 8041**, so there was no limit or date range at which it worked. Its only caller is `tools/ds_matchdb_mcp_server.py:347`, whose `_dispatch_tool` catches into an MCP error envelope - so the blast radius is "the `match_mode_stats` tool has always failed for TFT", not a crash. (2) **SQLite orders TEXT above INTEGER, so `'' > 0` is TRUE** and the `tft_placement > 0` predicate - whose whole job is to exclude rows with no placement - ADMITTED them.

**One of my own claims was REFUTED by measurement and is recorded as such.** I first reported that consequence (2) poisoned the `get_best_comps` ranking live, because an unplaced comp aggregates to `avg_place 0.0` and sorts FIRST under `ORDER BY avg_place ASC`. Probing the real data killed it: all **354** rows with a non-numeric placement are **ARAM 243 / ARENA 28 / SR 83 - zero are TFT**, so the `mode = 'TFT'` predicate shielded both TFT readers and `get_best_comps` returned sane output on live data. The hole is REAL and reproducible (a TFT row saved without a placement reaches it directly, which `test_unplaced_row_does_not_reach_best_comps_ranking` pins) but it was **LATENT, not active**. Cited that way and no wider.

**Fix (root-cause, one definition of correct).** `NUMERIC_COLS` is derived from the declared `_SCHEMA` affinity and split `_INT_COLS` / `_REAL_COLS`; numeric columns default to `0` and are coerced at bind time through `coerce_numeric`. Item 211's bespoke `game_id` int-coercion is subsumed. `test_numeric_column_set_matches_schema_affinity` reads `PRAGMA table_info` and fails if a future column is added with numeric affinity but not registered, so the coercion set cannot drift behind the schema. Two false docstring claims in the same file were also corrected (4a): the module usage example advertised `db.get_best_comps(min_placement=4, ...)` against a real signature of `(min_games=2, limit=10)` - a documented call that raises `TypeError`, now pinned by a test that parses the docstring and checks each kwarg against `inspect.signature`; and `close()` claimed other threads' connections "are released by the OS", which is wrong about the mechanism (CPython finalizes the orphaned `Connection`; the OS does not).

**Backfill - the half that made this more than a guard (CLAUDE.md "Data Fixes", charter 6e).** The writer fix stops NEW bad rows and does nothing for the **8395 of 8395** already written. `scripts/repair_match_db_column_types.py` repairs them THROUGH THE SAME `coerce_numeric` the writer binds through, deliberately not a hand-written `CAST`, so the repaired value is identical by construction rather than by agreement between two definitions. Idempotent, single-transaction, dry-run by default, and it intersects `NUMERIC_COLS` with `PRAGMA table_info` so a legacy short table is handled. **Executed against the live DB after a verified WAL-safe backup** (`Connection.backup()`, never copying the `.db` alone - the `-wal`/`-shm` sidecars are part of the database; backup verified 8395/8395 rows before applying). Result: **8395 rows repaired, 0 non-numeric cells remaining across all 15 numeric columns, row count unchanged at 8395, and a re-run reports "rows to fix: 0"**. `get_mode_stats("TFT", 20)` now returns `{'games': 20, ...}` where it previously raised; `get_mode_stats("ARAM")` is identical before and after, which is the control. Backup retained in the session scratchpad.

**Tests: 30 added across two new files, 21 of them mutation-tested.** `tests/test_match_db_column_types.py` (20 tests) and `tests/test_match_db_backfill.py` (10 tests) - all RED before the fix (33 failed / 13 passed on first run; the 13 that passed are the characterization tests, which is the point of writing them). **Six mutations run, five RED, and the one survivor is reported honestly as an EQUIVALENT MUTANT rather than papered over:** reverting the numeric default from `0` back to `""` left all 20 tests GREEN, because the bind-time coercion loop runs unconditionally over every numeric column and so the default provably cannot change behaviour (`reference_mutation_survivor_may_be_equivalent`). The behaviour-bearing guard is the coercion loop, and deleting THAT went red 35-failed. Dropping the repair's UPDATE, binding raw values instead of coerced ones, and ignoring `--apply` all went RED and restored green.

**Suites, observed THIS run from the repo root on the FINAL code: RC `tests/` 19258 passed / 2 failed / 144 skipped / 4498 subtests** (19228 before this cycle, so +30, exactly the tests added), **DS `agents/daemon_slayer/tests` 10684 passed / 13482 subtests, exit 0**, ruff `All checks passed!` repo-wide, 0 non-ASCII bytes and 0 CRLF in all four touched files. **The 2 failures are the SAME two inherited failures cycle 15 documented, and were re-PROVEN this run rather than carried forward:** neither file contains a single reference to `match_db` or `MatchDB` (`grep -c` returns 0 for both), `test_live_three_profiles` fails `'1.278.1' != '1.278.0'` because `lane/true-audit` is **26 commits behind `origin/main`**, which already carries `ENGINE_VERSION = "1.278.1"` (verified by `git show origin/main:agents/daemon_slayer/__init__.py`), so it resolves on merge; `test_cli_version_still_matches_the_pin` is a deliberate canary firing on CLI 2.1.251 against a 2.1.220 pin, and its own failure message forbids re-pinning without first re-running the negative control.

**No RC restart, and the reason is the item-1179 lesson, not laziness.** The running RC (pid 7788) executes MAIN-tree code, so a `restart_trigger.txt` bounce from this worktree would restart the OLD code and prove nothing - item 1179 is exactly the case of a lane fix that a restart did not deploy. The fix deploys on merge. **Consequence the merger must know:** until merge + restart the live RC keeps writing `''` rows, so `scripts/repair_match_db_column_types.py --apply` should be re-run once after the merge; it is idempotent and reported 0 rows to fix on re-run. Re-checked at wrap: still **0** non-numeric cells (RC has been idle in `client` mode, no game played since the repair).

1281. DONE **2026-08-30 (lane 8 Headless-True-Audit cycle 15: the L4 secret-file denylist on the LAN-reachable `:8890` server was inert against percent-encoding - `/%2Eenv` served `.env` that `/.env` correctly refused; Tier-1).** Target `agents/_supervisor_http.py` (961 lines, NOT frozen - `reference_two_parallel_supervisors_coexist` records that only `ops/rc_supervisor.py` is, per the s243 split). Chosen on criterion 1 (externally reachable input) and criterion 3 (threaded server), and because my own RM-321 named this file the worst of five `log_message` overrides. Confirmed NOT among the 14 files taken in cycles 1-14. **The bind was re-measured LIVE rather than inherited from that row:** `Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 8890,8891 -State Listen` reports both on `0.0.0.0`, pid 25908.

**CALIBRATION FIRST, recorded before reading the file. Two of four predictions were right, one was HALF-REFUTED and one was fully refuted.** Right: P1's scrub half, and P3's guess that the static-file path had a weakness. **P1 HALF-REFUTED:** I predicted the override dropped BOTH the control-char escaping and the peer address. It drops only the escaping - `log.info("web %s - %s", self.address_string(), ...)` already names the peer, so RM-321's own census ("peer yes, scrub NO") was accurate and my prediction over-claimed against it. The peer is now pinned by a test so a later edit cannot drop it. **P4 REFUTED:** I predicted an uncapped request body; `_read_body` already carries a 256 KiB cap and has since an earlier audit. The real body defect was a different one (W3 below).

**W1 SECURITY, the headline. The denylist and the file-opener disagreed about what the path IS.** `_is_forbidden` tested `self.path`, the RAW request target; `SimpleHTTPRequestHandler.translate_path` calls `urllib.parse.unquote` on that same target before opening the file. So percent-encoding any single character of a basename walked straight past the gate. **Measured against the real handler over a real socket, before any edit:** `/.env` -> 403, `/%2Eenv` -> 200 with `SECRET_KEY=...`; `/api-key-claude.txt` -> 403, `/api-key-claude%2Etxt` -> 200 with the key body; `/%61pi-key-claude.txt` -> 200, proving there is nothing special about the dot - any character will do.

**SEVERITY WAS CUT TWICE BY MEASUREMENT AND BOTH CUTS ARE KEPT HERE SO NOBODY RE-INFLATES THEM. This is a BROKEN SAFETY NET, not a live secret leak and not the item-1177 arbitrary-read class.** (1) It is CONFINED TO THE WEB ROOT: five escape vectors (`/../x`, `/%2E%2E/x`, `/..%2Fx`, `/%2e%2e%2fx`, `/....//x`) were all measured 403/404, because the stdlib `translate_path` collapses traversal correctly - so `API-Key-Claude.txt` at the repo root was never reachable and saying otherwise would be the cycle-13 error of grading a finding by its scariest available framing. (2) The real `web/` root was scanned and contains NO dotfile and no secret-shaped file today, so nothing was leaking. **What IS broken is exactly the control's stated purpose:** the class docstring says the denylist exists so "a misplaced `.env` in `web/` never reaches the wire, even inside the LAN" - the misplaced-file case is the operator error it was built to catch, and it did not catch it. A safety net that only works against the spelling nobody attacking would use is not a safety net.

**W2 MACHINE-ENV (RM-321 for this file).** `BaseHTTPRequestHandler.log_message` ends with `message.translate(self._control_char_table)`, a stdlib hardening that lives INSIDE the method so any override drops it with no warning and no lint. Measured against the real handler: `GET /<ESC>[31mFAKE-ADMIN-OK<ESC>[0m<BS><BS><DEL>` put raw `0x1b`, `0x08` and `0x7f` into the log record, at INFO, on the 0.0.0.0-bound port, where the backspaces erase characters when the operator reads `logs/YYYY-MM-DD.log` with cat or tail. Closed by reusing `dashboard._handler._scrub_log` rather than re-rolling it, which is what RM-321's acceptance asked for; that helper's fallback was verified in cycle 13 against all 1111998 non-surrogate codepoints. **The import direction was checked, not assumed:** `agents/` already imports from `dashboard/` in `agents/supervisor.py` and `agents/agent2_backend/file_ingest.py`, and `dashboard/_handler.py` imports nothing from `agents/`, so there is no cycle. RM-321's "wrong import direction" caveat was about `mc/`, which is deliberately decoupled and still is.

**W3 INPUT VALIDATION, the one I had not predicted.** Every body control keys off `Content-Length`. A `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` POST carries none, so `_read_body` returned `b""` and the route ran as though the client had sent `{}` - a body DISCARDED, not merely uncapped. Measured: a chunked request with a 23-byte payload yields `b""`. Now a 411. **The guard uses `get_all`, not `get`, and that is not a style choice:** cycle 13 measured that `email.message.Message.get` returns only the FIRST header of a repeated name, so `Transfer-Encoding: identity` followed by `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` walks past a `get`-based guard. A test asserts `headers.get(...) == "identity"` (the trap) while the guard still fires.

**SEVEN DIMENSIONS.** CORRECTNESS **HARDENED** (the class docstring's denylist claim was false as written; the code now matches it). SECURITY **HARDENED** (W1). ERROR-HANDLING **CLEAN, checked rather than assumed** - `_send_error` sends a fixed public message and logs the raw cause to the supervisor log only, and a grep for `str(e)` or an f-string interpolation of an exception into a wire body returns nothing, so the CLAUDE.md raw-error rule is already satisfied. RESOURCE-LIFETIME **CLEAN** - both `urlopen` calls use `with` and carry timeouts (1.5s, 2.0s), and the queue-log read uses `with`. CONCURRENCY **N/A** - this module writes no polled file, holds no lock and touches no SQLite; per-connection isolation is `ThreadingTCPServer`'s existing design. INPUT-VALIDATION **HARDENED** (W3). MACHINE-ENV **HARDENED** (W2).

**Tests: `tests/test_supervisor_http_lane8_cycle15.py`, 18 tests, the module's first dedicated coverage, RED FIRST at 5 failed / 6 passed.** Every guard drives the REAL handler over a REAL socket where the behaviour is socket-shaped. **EIGHT mutants planted in the final round, ALL EIGHT KILLED**, each anchor asserted to apply EXACTLY ONCE and the source restored byte-identical by sha256 after every round. The full round was re-run from scratch after the verifier pass, because the production fix itself changed. **The mutation run earned its keep twice, and both are process findings, not code findings.** (1) **M4 SURVIVED on the first pass** - the backslash normalisation in the gate was an untested guard, `feedback_guard_on_nondefault_call_path_is_untested` exactly. Rather than write a leak-shaped assertion, I measured whether it was an EQUIVALENT mutant and it is not quite: the stdlib DROPS any segment whose `os.path.dirname` is non-empty (measured, `os.path.dirname("x\\.env")` is `"x"` on Windows), so no file is served either way, but the GATE's own answer changes from 403 to a fall-through. The test therefore pins the gate's contract at unit level and its docstring says plainly that it is NOT preventing a leak the stdlib already prevents - a leak-shaped test there would have passed with the guard deleted. (2) **M7 was added only because I noticed my chunked tests all called `_rejects_chunked` directly and nothing proved `do_POST` invoked it.** Deleting the call from `do_POST` would have left every unit test green. The wiring test uses an unrouted path so the 411 is distinguishable from routing's 404 and no handler (and no LLM spawn) runs.

**THE HARNESS ALSO CAUGHT ITSELF, and it is the most transferable thing here.** The first mutation run aborted on `RESTORE FAILED` after M1: `Path.write_text` had rewritten the whole 961-line file from LF to CRLF, so the sha256 restore check failed even though the TEXT was correct - `reference_windows_write_text_crlf_byte_count`, hit live. The file was normalised back to LF and the harness switched to `read_bytes`/`write_bytes`. **Without the sha check the run would have continued and silently committed a 961-line line-ending churn on top of a 40-line fix.** The exactly-once anchor assertion and the byte-level restore check are both cheap and both fired this run.

**THE VERIFIER FOUND A DEFECT IN THE FIX, WHICH IS THE ARGUMENT FOR RUNNING AN ADVERSARIAL PASS AGAINST YOUR OWN WORK.** It CONFIRMED all nine claims put to it, matched both suite counts exactly, reproduced the original bypass on `git show HEAD:` code, found FOUR bypass vectors I had not (`/%2E%65%6Ev`, `/secrets%2Ejson`, `/sub%2F%2Eenv`, and the `?query` / `#fragment` forms), and cleared the confinement claim far harder than I had - **30 escape vectors** including `%c0%ae` overlong UTF-8, `%00` truncation, `..;/`, UNC `//127.0.0.1/c$/`, absolute `C:/Windows/win.ini` and double-encoded forms, with the outside-webroot canary appearing in ZERO responses. **Then it refuted a claim in my own code comment.** I had written that normalising `\` to `/` kept `_is_forbidden` "from ever being LOOSER than the opener". The verifier also caught the RM-229 sibling row citing a wrong line number; it is corrected, the second site it missed is now recorded too, and the row says to locate both by string rather than by line.

The client set for `:8890`/`:8891` is unmeasured, lane 8 runs with no operator present to ask whether the Phase 3 UI is opened from another device, and a bind flip is exactly the change a headless suite cannot validate.
